note: Decoded-frame cache A/B on the dedicated A100. StreamingVideoReader.seek has one fast path, frame_index == current_index + 1; the renderer asks each reader for [c-2 .. c+2] per item, so the next item's first request is c-1, a one-frame backward step that re-decodes from the preceding keyframe at keyint 250. BOTH arms mounted the identical patched reader file, so the only difference between them is the RENDER_FRAME_CACHE environment variable. The cache-off arm ran FIRST and into a fresher output directory, and both of those confounds make the cache-on arm look worse, so the measured effect is a floor rather than a ceiling. Stage figures are means over the same three clips, deduplicated per log because each timing line is printed twice.

fixture.note: Local CPU fixture: a real H.264 clip at keyint 250, replaying the dataset's own index pattern over 300 frames. Counts transfer, milliseconds do not.

outputDiff.note: Pixel comparisons. The identicalConfig rows are every comparison of two runs of the SAME configuration measured in this work; they are the population the treatment has to be read against, not zero. Worst pixel is a maximum over 751 frames and every pixel -- an extreme-value statistic, heavy-tailed, and a poor discriminator at this sample size; meanAbs and psnr are the robust ones.

seekExactness.note: Direct test of the hypothesis that the cached and uncached readers disagree about what frame i is, because OpenCV's frame-index seek is widely reported inexact on H.264. Each index was fetched twice from a real pipeline output: once by reading forward from the start, once by a backward seek. REFUTED -- seeking is frame-exact here, which is what generalises the cache's exactness to any access pattern.
